title: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938)
summary: The federal court had to apply state law, including state decisional law, rather than create its own general common-law negligence rule.
notes:
Erie is not a rule that every state procedure applies in federal court. York, Byrd, Hanna, and Shady Grove examine the later questions. Nor does it abolish specialized federal common law supported by distinct federal interests.

Tompkins, a Pennsylvania citizen, was struck by something protruding from a passing Erie train while walking on a footpath beside the tracks at night, and sued in the Southern District of New York (Erie being a New York corporation); Justice Brandeis wrote for the Court, declaring that there is no federal general common law.

Vote detail: Justice Reed concurred in part (statutory ground only); Justice Butler dissented, joined by Justice McReynolds; Justice Cardozo did not participate.

sections.Parties: Tompkins, a Pennsylvania citizen injured by a train, sued Erie Railroad in federal court in New York on a diversity basis.
sections.Material Facts: Tompkins was walking alongside railroad tracks in Pennsylvania when a passing train injured him. The parties disputed the legal duty owed to a person in his position. Pennsylvania law allegedly treated him as a trespasser for whom a more demanding showing of wrongful conduct was required. Under Swift, the federal courts instead used a general common-law rule that supported recovery. The jury awarded Tompkins $30,000.
sections.Procedural History: The federal trial court and court of appeals allowed recovery under the general-law approach. The Supreme Court overruled Swift, reversed, and remanded for application of the appropriate state law. It did not itself enter a final merits judgment absolving the railroad.
sections.Issue: Could a federal diversity court disregard the state’s judicially stated substantive rule in favor of its own view of general common law?
sections.Holding: No. Except in matters governed by federal constitutional or statutory authority, state law supplies the rule of decision, including law stated through state judicial decisions.
sections.Reasoning: The Court examined the failure of Swift’s hoped-for uniformity and the resulting opportunity for forum shopping. Identical conduct could have different legal consequences depending on whether a litigant qualified for and selected federal court. That inequality distorted the allocation of authority and advantaged parties able to manipulate citizenship or forum choice. The Court also reinterpreted the Rules of Decision Act and identified constitutional limits on federal creation of general substantive law in areas committed to the states. State common law was no less law because it came from judicial decisions rather than a statute. The opinion therefore changed both the source a diversity court must consult and the explanation of its institutional role.

learning.why: The federal court had to apply state law, including state decisional law, rather than create its own general common-law negligence rule.

topics.cp-erie: A federal court could not replace applicable state common law with a supposed federal general common law.
topics.cp-federalism: The opinion tied the governing-law problem to the allocation of state and federal lawmaking authority.
topics.cp-forum-shopping: The Swift regime allowed litigants to obtain different substantive law by selecting a federal forum.
topics.cp-precedent: State judicial decisions can state the law binding on a federal court applying state law.
topics.cp-erie-history: Erie overruled Swift v. Tyson and is the pivot of the Swift-to-Erie narrative.
topics.cp-usc-1652: The decision reinterprets 'laws of the several states' in the Rules of Decision Act to include state judicial decisions.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Reed agreed with the result on statutory grounds and did not embrace the same constitutional analysis. Justices Butler and McReynolds objected to the Court’s reaching the constitutional issue in the way it did.

mnemonic.rationale: A man struck by a passing train
